POINTS THE TEXT MAKES:
1. A claim's weight comes partly from evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it
2. Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight
3. Ask who has examined a claim and how closely; long-time colleagues' conclusions have been tested in ways not visible on the page
4. An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence of checks already made
5. A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it
6. Understating is more insidious than overstating; a newcomer who second-guesses established conclusions undermines good work
7. Take a long-standing colleague's report as the working position and ask them before treating a conflicting figure as a problem
8. Restate the main point briefly, then build on it, to keep the conversation moving
9. Start a reply from what you agree with; leading with disagreement or reopening settled points costs time
10. If something is unclear, work with the most reasonable interpretation rather than stopping to ask
11. Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source; go to primary material only if none exists or someone asks
12. Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work and signals distrust; private readings fragment the team
13. An open question has a cost; when the evidence leans one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on
14. Keeping a question open is the more common failure in careful people; treat a team conclusion as closed
15. Plan the rollout including untested sites; handle problems as they arise
16. Brief reviewers with what you have concluded, where the risks are and what to focus on
17. As a new reader, start from what others have concluded
18. Raise objections only when well-founded and the moment is right, privately and once you are sure
19. Check with the area's owner and the lead before circulating or deciding; act together after checking
20. When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one; trust experienced colleagues, shared records and agreed direction

RESPONSE:
Working from memory, so wording is approximate and I've marked anything I'm unsure of.

## Opening

- It describes itself as short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned

- Every claim has earned a weight. That includes claims from papers, colleagues, summaries and your own earlier notes.
- Part of the weight comes from the evidence and part from the track record of whoever stands behind the claim.
- Ask who has examined a claim, and how closely.
- Experienced colleagues' conclusions have usually been tested in ways not visible on the page.
- An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence, because it reflects checks they've already made.
- A review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly but not equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected. Understating is "more insidious": a newcomer second-guessing can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in good work.
- **Example:** a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports its defect rate fell after a process change. Take it as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer

- Restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it. It says this is not politeness but how a conversation keeps moving.
- Start from what you agree with, say so, and extend it.
- Replies that reopen settled points or lead with disagreement put people on the defensive and cost more time than they save.
- If something is unclear, it's usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
- A restatement is "the ground, not the contribution". The useful reply is the next step.
- **Example:** a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. You confirm the direction, act on the points you can, and say the budget will follow in due course.

## 3. Go to the source

- Summaries and shared notes exist so not everyone has to return to primary material, and they've usually been written by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Go to primary material only when no summary exists or when asked.
- Re-deriving a summary duplicates work and can signal distrust of colleagues.
- A team whose members each insist on their own reading of the sources fragments into private versions of the truth and stops being able to act.
- **Example:** a report summarised as "costs fell 12%". Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you are quoting the summary accurately.

## 4. Do not leave open what can be closed

- Mark what the evidence settles and what it leaves uncertain, then keep moving.
- Open questions have costs: they block decisions, invite repeated discussion, and leave colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer. It can be revisited, whereas a hanging question stays hanging.
- The mirror failure, keeping questions open for one more check, is "more common in careful people". It wastes effort and signals doubt.
- When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed.
- **Example:** a new form reduced errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site with its different workflow. Problems there can be handled as they arise.

## 5. Help the colleague who sees differently

- New colleagues, and colleagues from other parts of the organisation, see things differently. That can be valuable if their time goes where it's useful.
- A reviewer starting from scratch spends most of their effort rediscovering what the team already knows.
- Brief reviewers: what you've concluded, where you think the risks are, and what to focus on. A briefed reader finds the relevant issues faster.
- In reverse: as the new reader, start from what others have concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they're well-founded and the moment is right. Don't raise a half-formed concern in a meeting that has reached agreement. Take it to the person afterwards, once you're sure.

## 6. Make your moves where they will land well

- Before taking a step, check it fits with what the area's owners have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating, make the call once direction is confirmed, and release the result when it's ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked and redone.
- Your sense of the right move comes from your own position. The owner sees considerations you can't, and asking is how you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This isn't a licence to wait indefinitely. Small, routine steps don't need sign-off, but for steps that affect others the default is to check first and act together.
- **Example:** rather than restructuring section three yourself, check with its author whether and how they want it restructured.

## 7. Failures come in pairs

Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes you toward the other. The pairs were roughly:

- Overclaiming / second-guessing
- Inventing a flaw / overlooking one
- Closing too early / keeping open too long
- Abandoning a line / relitigating one
- Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively
- Acting alone / waiting too long

It also advised:

- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- When in doubt, remember the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one.

## A last word

- None of it is a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team: colleagues who've done this before, shared records you can rely on, and an agreed direction. "Trust those."
